sections.title: Policy and access to the centre
sections.text:
Leipzig manages little of its parking, and the debate is about doing more. A Green council motion of 20 November 2025 asks for at least 5% of parking space to be managed by 2030 and 10% by 2035, up from 2.3% today, and for resident fees to rise gradually to €365 per vehicle from 2030. The administration proposed deferring specific decisions until its long-term parking concept comes before the council [1]. In April 2026 a local newspaper reported that the city's transport office supported extending resident parking in three stages, starting with the rest of Mitte and then districts above 90% occupancy such as Plagwitz and Gohlis-Süd. The annual resident fee is still €30.70 and has not changed for many years. This is a proposal, not a decision [0]. In 2024 the council backed the administration's view that it has no legal basis for fees scaled by vehicle size [2]. An August 2020 proposal to raise on-street tariffs in the centre to €1.50 per half hour does not say what was finally adopted [3].

The city's 2023 survey found car trips at 31% of daily trips, down from 36.5% in 2018, with walking at 33% [5]. In April 2026 Leipzig said it is to lift its Umweltzone, in place since 2011, through the update of its air quality plan, because legal limits have been met at all official stations since 2019 [4]. In May 2025 the council unanimously approved further examination of a CDU proposal to let residents park in shopping-centre car parks in the evening and at weekends [20].

sections.title: Parking developments
sections.text:
Park-and-ride is where the city has acted. The 2020 mobility strategy lists improvements to existing park-and-ride sites, new sites 'especially in the south' and digitisation, all as planned measures [7]. A CDU motion approved in November 2020 asked that charging for park-and-ride parking be examined, with the parking ticket allowing free use of public transport [8]. In autumn 2023 the city and LVB began testing a real-time display of free park-and-ride spaces covering 814 spaces at six sites [9], and the administration confirmed budget funding from 2026 for a new site at S-Bahnhof Heiterblick [10]. The lots are free and promoted for the Christmas market and for RB Leipzig matches [11][12].

The central garages are private. A city leaflet of 2022 says garages and car parks in the centre are privately operated, with free-space counts on its guidance signs. It lists Augustusplatz (1,244 spaces), the Zoo (1,350), Höfe am Brühl (820), Hauptbahnhof Promenaden West (686) and East (574) and the Petersbogen (554) among others [13]. Höfe am Brühl charges €2.50 per hour with an €18 daily maximum [14], and the Petersbogen is APCOA's, at €2.60 per hour [19]. Q-Park lists five Leipzig facilities [18], and Paunsdorf Center, out of town, offers 4,400 free spaces [15]. A June 2024 article citing Leipziger Stadtwerke put the city at about 350 publicly accessible stations with about 700 charging points [21]. We found no sourced figures on a shift from the centre to shopping centres.

sections.title: Operators, positioning and utilisation
sections.text:
Our price data cover 17 garages with 6,626 spaces within 2 km of Augustusplatz. Five are within 500 m (1,972 spaces) and ten more within 1 km (4,258). Q-Park has five of them (2,032 spaces) at a median of €2.50 an hour, APCOA five (1,168, €2.60), ECE two at the station (1,260, €2.00), plus Contipark, B+B and a Goldbeck-run coach-terminal garage at €1.50 an hour. Prices cluster between €2.00 and €2.60 an hour for the larger central garages. We do not measure occupancy in any of them.

What we do measure are four park-and-ride lots 6 to 9 km from the centre, with 2,300 spaces in our feed. Occupancy over August to early October 2026 averaged 18% on weekdays and 13% at weekends. P+R Lausen is the fullest (29% on weekdays, 450 spaces), then Plovdiver Straße (22%) and Leipziger Messe (18% of 1,200 spaces). Schönauer Ring is almost unused (2%). The city's own display project counts 814 spaces at six sites, so our percentages for the lots, which use larger capacities, should be read with care. The data cover the summer holidays, so term-time figures may differ, and we have no multi-year history for Leipzig.
